key: Through all this world strode Visnu; thrice his foot he planted, and the whole Was gathered in his footstep’s dust.
s: Near the close of a hymn calling a round of gods to the rite, six verses turn to Vishnu and his strides; Sāyaṇa, on 1.22.17, reads it of Vishnu in his descent as Trivikrama, the three-strider, whose dusty footprint held the whole visible world.

evidence.gloss: Vishnu, bearing the Trivikrama descent (avatāra), strode in a special striding over this whole world that appears to us. Then he set down his foot in three ways. In the dusty place of this Vishnu’s foot this whole world was completely contained.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref 1.22.17, at [21,17]). Hymn 1.22 has 21 verses and 1.22.16 to 1.22.21 all speak of Vishnu, so ‘near the close ... six verses turn to Vishnu and his strides’ is faithful. Sāyaṇa on 1.22.17 names Vishnu trivikramāvatāradhārī, says he strode over this whole perceived world (idaṃ pratīyamānaṃ sarvaṃ jagat) and that in the dusty place of his foot (pāṃsure dhūliyukte pādasthāne) this whole world was fully contained; on 1.22.16 he again speaks of the three steps in the Trivikrama avatāra. Wilson’s note confirms ‘Sayana conceives the text to allude to the Trivikrama Avatara’. ‘the three-strider’ is only the gloss of the name.
